The African black duck (Anas sparsa) inhabits fast-flowing streams and rivers across sub-Saharan Africa, where it exhibits life-history traits characteristic of a relatively slow-paced, long-lived waterfowl species. Newly hatched ducklings emerge from eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], with the incubation period lasting approximately 32 days [ab = approximately 32 days]. Upon hatching, the precocial chicks are capable of leaving the nest within hours and weigh around 35 grams [Wwb = around 35 grams], a modest neonatal mass that reflects the substantial yolk reserves these birds rely upon during their first days of life and that represents only a small fraction of the adult size they will ultimately attain. This initial body mass contrasts markedly with the several hundred grams these birds will reach as adults, and the downy young begin foraging for aquatic invertebrates almost immediately under the watchful guidance of both parents. The rapid development of thermoregulatory capacity in these chicks is facilitated by the warm incubation temperatures experienced during embryogenesis.

Pronounced sexual dimorphism is evident in adult body mass, with mature females reaching an ultimate wet weight of 930 grams [Wwi = 930 grams], while males, which are substantially heavier, attain approximately 1100 grams [Wwi = approximately 1100 grams], a difference likely reflecting the energetic demands of territorial defense and courtship displays along their linear riverine territories. These mass values are consistent with those recorded for other members of the genus Anas that occupy similar lotic habitats. The relatively large body size of this species, compared to many other African ducks, may confer advantages in terms of predator avoidance and the ability to exploit deeper, swifter foraging waters that smaller congeners cannot access. Field studies based on mark-recapture data indicate that body condition, measured as mass relative to structural size, fluctuates seasonally in response to food availability and the energetic costs of breeding.

The timing of developmental milestones in Anas sparsa reflects a strategy that balances the need for extended parental care against the constraints of seasonal resource availability. Young birds attain flight capability and achieve nutritional independence at approximately 63 days after hatching [tx = approximately 63 days after hatching], a relatively prolonged fledging period compared to many temperate-nesting dabbling ducks. This extended dependency phase allows the developing chicks to refine their foraging skills and build sufficient body reserves before venturing out on their own. The fledging age of 63 days after hatching [tx = 63 days after hatching] is closely tied to the predictable seasonal emergence of aquatic insect prey in the fast-flowing streams these birds inhabit. Following fledging, juveniles remain in family groups for several additional weeks before dispersing to establish their own territories, a process that can take many months given the linear, often saturated nature of suitable riverine habitats.

Sexual maturation in the African black duck is a gradual process, with young birds typically reaching puberty at 189 days after hatching [tp = 189 days after hatching]. This relatively early onset of gonadal development, compared to the actual timing of first reproduction, suggests that social factors and territory availability may act as important constraints on breeding. First-year birds frequently exhibit courtship behaviors and pair formation during their first dry season but may not successfully produce a clutch until they have secured a stable section of stream with adequate food resources and cover. The age at first successful brood in this species, based on data from a closely related congener Anas platyrhynchos used as a comparative reference, is estimated at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching]. This pattern of early puberty followed by deferred reproduction is common among waterfowl inhabiting stable, resource-predictable environments.

Reproductive output in the African black duck is relatively modest, with females laying between 4 and 8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 4 and 8 eggs per clutch] and producing only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This conservative reproductive strategy, yielding at most one brood annually, stands in contrast to many temperate-nesting ducks that may produce two or even three clutches per season. Maximum recorded longevity in the wild for Anas sparsa remains poorly documented, but extrapolating from data on the closely related mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) suggests a potential lifespan of approximately 10,622 days [am = approximately 10,622 days]. This extensive lifespan, combined with low annual reproductive output, aligns with a slow life-history strategy typical of large-bodied waterfowl inhabiting relatively stable, low-predation environments. The combination of extended parental care, deferred first reproduction, and low annual fecundity underscores the importance of adult survival in maintaining population stability in this long-lived riverine specialist.
